summary: Documents version 2 of OSPF, a link-state routing protocol in which routers share information about their links to compute paths inside a network. It was replaced by RFC 2178.

eli5.summary: Every router draws a map of the whole neighborhood from what neighbors tell it, then finds the best route on its own.

questions: what is the ospf designated router
subtitle: How routers inside one network share link maps, each compute their own shortest paths, and recover quickly from failures.

tldr.problem: Distance-vector routing protocols of the time (Bellman-Ford based) were slow to react to topology changes. Larger networks needed faster convergence, subnet and Type of Service support, and authenticated routing updates.
tldr.mechanism: Every OSPF router floods descriptions of its own links, called link state advertisements, so that all routers in an area hold an identical database. Each router then runs a shortest-path calculation with itself as the root to build its routing table. Areas hide detail to limit traffic.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1583 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1247 with backward-compatible fixes and was itself obsoleted by RFC 2178.

today: RFC 1583 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1247 and has itself been obsoleted by RFC 2178, so it should be read as a historical stage of OSPF version 2 rather than the current specification.

sections.title: What OSPF Is and Why It Exists
sections.content:
RFC 1583 specifies version 2 of the Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) protocol. OSPF is an Interior Gateway Protocol: it distributes routing information between routers that belong to a single Autonomous System. It is based on link-state (SPF) technology, which the RFC describes as a departure from the Bellman-Ford base used by traditional TCP/IP routing protocols.

It was designed expressly for the TCP/IP internet. The RFC lists explicit support for IP subnetting, Type of Service (TOS) based routing and the tagging of externally derived routes. It also provides authentication of routing updates, uses IP multicast for them, and aims to respond quickly to topology changes with small amounts of routing traffic.

OSPF routes IP packets based only on the destination address and the IP Type of Service. Packets are routed as they are, with no extra encapsulation as they cross the Autonomous System. This memo replaces RFC 1247; the differences are backward-compatible bug fixes and clarifications.
sections.eli5: OSPF is a way for the routers inside one big network to tell each other which roads are open, so every packet can find a good route. It reacts quickly when a road closes.

sections.title: The Topological Database and Shortest-Path Tree
sections.content:
Each router keeps a database that describes the Autonomous System as a directed graph. The vertices are routers and networks. An edge joins two routers connected by a point-to-point network, and an edge between a router and a network means the router has an interface on that network. Vertices come in three types: router, network and stub network, and only the first two can carry transit traffic.

A cost is attached to the output side of each router interface and is set by the administrator; the lower the cost, the more likely the interface is used. Each piece of the database is a link state advertisement describing one router or network neighborhood. All routers run the same algorithm in parallel and each builds a shortest-path tree with itself as root. Only the next hop to a destination is used for forwarding.

Externally derived routes (from EGP or static configuration) are flooded unaltered and appear as leaves on the tree. Type 1 external metrics are comparable to link state metrics, so the cost to the advertising router is added. Type 2 external metrics are treated as greater than any internal path, so the smallest external metric wins and internal distance only breaks ties. If both kinds exist, Type 1 takes precedence. An external advertisement may carry a forwarding address so traffic can go straight to the real next hop and skip an extra hop through the AS boundary router.

When several equal-cost routes exist they are all discovered and used. OSPF can also calculate separate routes per IP TOS if separate interface costs are configured, though a cost for TOS 0 must always be specified and routers may be configured to use TOS 0 only.
sections.eli5: Imagine every kid in a school draws the same map of the hallways, with a number on each hallway for how long it takes to walk. Each kid then finds their own quickest path from where they sit.

sections.title: Splitting the Network into Areas
sections.content:
OSPF lets contiguous networks and hosts be grouped into an area. Each area runs its own copy of the link-state algorithm and has its own database. The inside of an area is invisible from outside, and routers inside know nothing of the detail outside. The RFC says this isolation marks a reduction in routing traffic, and also protects intra-area routing from bad routing data injected from elsewhere.

Area 0.0.0.0 is the backbone. It must be contiguous, and it carries traffic between areas. A packet between areas travels in three pieces: an intra-area path to an area border router, a backbone path, and an intra-area path to the destination. If the backbone is split, the administrator restores it with virtual links across a common non-backbone (transit) area. A virtual link is treated like an unnumbered point-to-point network, and its cost is not configured but is the intra-area path cost between its two endpoints.

Routers fall into four overlapping classes: internal routers, area border routers (attached to multiple areas, and summarizing each area for the backbone), backbone routers and AS boundary routers (which exchange routing information with other Autonomous Systems).

An area is defined as a list of address ranges, each an address and mask pair. Area border routers advertise at most one summary route per range, at the minimum cost to any network in it. Every route carries a mask, which gives variable-length subnetting, and packets follow the longest (most specific) match.

Stub areas keep AS external advertisements out. Routing to outside destinations is done with a default route that an area border router injects via a summary advertisement. Virtual links cannot be configured through stub areas and AS boundary routers cannot be internal to them. OSPF does not try to repair a partitioned area; each piece simply becomes a separate area and the backbone routes between them.
sections.eli5: A big city is split into neighborhoods. People in one neighborhood know their own streets in detail, and only a main road tells them how to get to other neighborhoods.

sections.title: Neighbors, Adjacencies and the Designated Router
sections.content:
A router finds neighbors with the Hello Protocol. Hello packets are sent periodically out every interface. On broadcast and point-to-point networks they go to the multicast address AllSPFRouters, so neighbors are found dynamically. Non-broadcast networks need some configuration. Communication is known to be bidirectional when a router sees itself listed in a neighbor's Hello. Routers on a network must agree on the network mask, HelloInterval and RouterDeadInterval, or no neighbor relationship forms.

Not every pair of neighbors becomes adjacent. Adjacent routers synchronize databases: each describes its database in Database Description packets, in a master/slave poll and response exchange, and then requests the newer advertisements it is missing with Link State Requests. When all requests are satisfied the routers are fully adjacent, and the adjacency is advertised.

On every multi-access network a Designated Router (DR) originates a network links advertisement listing the attached routers and becomes adjacent to all other routers there. This reduces the adjacencies needed and shrinks the database. A router that comes up accepts an existing DR regardless of Router Priority, so the DR changes rarely. A Backup Designated Router is also adjacent to everyone, so if the DR fails the switch does not need new database synchronization. A Router Priority of 0 makes a router ineligible.
sections.eli5: Neighbors first say hello to check they can hear each other. Then they swap notes until both have the same map. On a busy street, one chosen helper (and a backup) collects everyone's news so each person does not have to talk to everybody else.

sections.title: The Neighbor State Machine
sections.content:
Each conversation with a neighbor has a state. The states run in order of progressing functionality: Down, Attempt (non-broadcast networks only), Init, 2-Way, ExStart, Exchange, Loading and Full.

Init means a Hello was seen but the router did not appear in it yet. 2-Way means communication is bidirectional, and the (Backup) Designated Router is chosen from neighbors in this state or higher. ExStart decides who is master and the initial sequence number; from here on the conversation is called an adjacency. In Exchange the databases are described, and in Loading missing advertisements are requested. In Full the routers are fully adjacent and the adjacency appears in router links and network links advertisements.

Events such as KillNbr, InactivityTimer and LLDown always force the neighbor back to Down, and SeqNumberMismatch or BadLSReq force it back to ExStart.
sections.eli5: It is like making a friend: you notice each other, wave, make sure you both see the wave, then trade stories until you know the same things. Then you are real friends.

sections.title: Packets and Advertisements
sections.content:
OSPF runs directly over IP using protocol number 89, with no transport layer. It relies on IP fragmentation only if needed, and recommends avoiding it. Packets should be sent with IP TOS 0, given preference over data traffic, and carry the IP precedence value Internetwork Control. Packets other than Hellos go only over adjacencies, so they travel a single IP hop, except over virtual links.

Every packet starts with a standard 24-byte header holding the version (2), type, packet length, Router ID, Area ID, checksum, an authentication type and a 64-bit authentication field. There are five packet types: Hello (1), Database Description (2), Link State Request (3), Link State Update (4) and Link State Acknowledgment (5).

There are five types of link state advertisement (LSA), all starting with a common 20-byte header: router links (1), network links (2), summary links to networks (3), summary links to AS boundary routers (4) and AS external links (5). Router and network links stay in one area; summary links are originated by area border routers; external links are originated by AS boundary routers and flood throughout the AS, except into stub areas.
sections.eli5: There are five kinds of messages, such as hello, here is what I know, please send me that, and thanks, got it. Each starts with a label saying who sent it and what kind it is.

sections.title: Flooding and Aging
sections.content:
Link State Update packets carry advertisements one hop further from where they were originated, and every advertisement is acknowledged separately in Link State Acknowledgment packets, which makes flooding reliable. For each received advertisement a router validates its checksum, discards unknown types, drops AS external ones in stub areas, and then compares it with its database copy.

Which instance is newer is decided by the LS sequence number first, then the larger LS checksum, then an instance at MaxAge, then by age if the two differ by more than MaxAgeDiff. A newer one is installed and flooded on; if it is the same instance it can count as an implied acknowledgment; an older one is discarded. Installing a changed advertisement can trigger a routing table recalculation.

Each advertisement has an LS age in seconds. A router refreshes its own advertisements every LSRefreshTime (30 minutes), will not originate a given one more often than MinLSInterval (5 seconds), and an advertisement that reaches MaxAge (1 hour) is flushed by reflooding. A router may flush its own advertisements early by setting the age to MaxAge, called premature aging, and it may never do so for other routers' advertisements. The LS checksum is verified whenever the age reaches a multiple of CheckAge (5 minutes).
sections.eli5: When something changes, you tell your neighbors, who tell theirs, and everybody says thanks so you know the message arrived. Old news gets a date stamp, and anything too old is thrown away.

sections.title: Building the Routing Table
sections.content:
A router rebuilds its routing table from scratch in five steps. First the old table is invalidated and saved to find changes. Second, intra-area routes come from the shortest-path tree of each attached area. Third, inter-area routes come from summary link advertisements (an area border router looks only at backbone summaries). Fourth, area border routers attached to transit areas examine those areas' summaries for better paths. Fifth, routes to external destinations come from AS external advertisements, using the AS boundary router locations found earlier. Each step may be repeated for non-zero TOS values.

Advertisements at MaxAge are not used in the calculation. When forwarding, a packet is matched against the table and the best (longest) match wins; if no path exists for a non-zero TOS, the packet follows the TOS 0 path.
sections.eli5: The router starts a fresh page and works out nearby places first, then places in other neighborhoods, and last places outside the city, so every address has a next step.

sections.title: Authentication and Differences from RFC 1247
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section is short: all OSPF protocol exchanges are authenticated, using the authentication fields in the packet header. The authentication type is configured per area, and the authentication data per interface. Two types are defined: 0 for no authentication and 1 for a simple password, a 64-bit value configured per network that every packet on that network must carry. This guards against routers inadvertently joining the area. The password is effectively sent in the clear. All other types are reserved for assignment by the IANA.

Appendix E lists the changes from RFC 1247, all backward-compatible, so implementations of both interoperate. The main fixes are for routing loops that certain virtual link configurations could cause (using a new V bit in router links advertisements), and for supporting supernetting and subnet 0 by letting host bits be set in a Link State ID to tell apart advertisements for networks with the same address but different masks.
sections.eli5: Routers share a secret password, and a router that does not know it cannot join the conversation. It is a simple lock, not a strong one.

fields.desc: The area the packet belongs to; virtual link packets use backbone 0.0.0.0.
